summary: Pyridostigmine bromide is an orally administered reversible cholinesterase inhibitor useful in the treatment of myasthenia gravis. By inhibiting acetylcholinesterase it permits freer transmission of nerve impulses across the neuromuscular junction, improving muscle strength. Compared with neostigmine it has a longer duration of action and fewer gastrointestinal side effects. Dosing is highly individualized, and overdose can precipitate a cholinergic crisis that must be distinguished from myasthenic crisis.

moa: Pyridostigmine bromide inhibits the destruction of acetylcholine by cholinesterase, thereby permitting freer transmission of nerve impulses across the neuromuscular junction. It is an analog of neostigmine but has a longer duration of action and produces fewer gastrointestinal side effects.

relative: Caution with concomitant atropine used to counteract side effects
monitor: Signs of cholinergic excess (muscarinic and nicotinic)

preg: The safety of pyridostigmine bromide during pregnancy in humans has not been established. Use in women who may become pregnant requires weighing the drug's potential benefits against the possible hazards to mother and child.
lact: The safety of pyridostigmine bromide during lactation in humans has not been established; use with caution, weighing benefit against potential risk to the infant.
renal: Pyridostigmine is mainly excreted unchanged by the kidney. Lower doses may be required in patients with renal disease, and treatment should be based on titration of drug dosage to effect.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is described in the labeling.

major: Depolarizing neuromuscular blockers (e.g. succinylcholine) - effects may be altered/prolonged
Other cholinergic/anticholinesterase agents - additive cholinergic toxicity risk
moderate: Anticholinergic agents (including atropine) - antagonize effect and may mask early signs of cholinergic excess
Aminoglycosides and other drugs with neuromuscular effects - may worsen weakness
interactions.food: May be taken with food to reduce gastrointestinal upset
interactions.diagnostics: Edrophonium (Tensilon) testing may be used to distinguish cholinergic from myasthenic crisis

serious: Cholinergic crisis (increasing muscle weakness, including respiratory muscles)
rare: Skin rash (bromide-related), usually resolving on discontinuation

Signs of cholinergic excess (salivation, sweating, diarrhea, fasciculations)

counsel: Take this medicine exactly as prescribed and time doses so you are strongest when you need to be
Lack of improvement can mean too little OR too much medicine - report worsening weakness, do not increase the dose yourself
Get urgent help if you have increasing weakness, breathing difficulty, severe cramping, drooling, or sweating
Tell your clinician if you have asthma, bowel or bladder obstruction, or heart rhythm problems
Keep tablets dry with the silica gel packet and in the original container
pk: Peak effect within a few hours
Longer duration of action than neostigmine; effect typically 3-6 hours
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); keep dry with enclosed silica gel in original container
pearls: First-line symptomatic treatment of myasthenia gravis - improves transmission at the neuromuscular junction
Cholinergic crisis (overdose) mimics myasthenic crisis (undertreatment) - both cause weakness; use edrophonium test and clinical judgment to distinguish
Cholinergic crisis calls for STOPPING all anticholinesterases; atropine controls muscarinic effects but not the weakness - support ventilation
Use with particular caution in bronchial asthma and avoid in mechanical intestinal/urinary obstruction
Reduce dose in renal impairment - drug is mainly excreted unchanged in urine
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose - do not double up. Because both underdosing and overdosing cause weakness, do not adjust the dose yourself; contact your clinician if symptoms worsen.
overdose: Overdosage produces a cholinergic crisis - muscarinic effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, increased salivation, bronchial secretions, miosis, sweating) and nicotinic effects (muscle cramps, fasciculations, and increasing weakness) that can involve the respiratory muscles and lead to death. Treatment requires prompt withdrawal of all drugs of this type, immediate use of atropine for muscarinic effects (used cautiously), maintenance of a patent airway and assisted ventilation/oxygen as needed; distinguish from myasthenic crisis (which needs more anticholinesterase) using edrophonium and clinical judgment.
